heading: Travel and Expense Policy
chunks.title: Travel and Expense Policy

chunks.body:
## Overview

This policy applies to every Larkspur Analytics employee who travels for work. Book travel through the Wayfare portal so that the finance team can see every commitment before it is paid. Trips that are booked outside the portal are reimbursed only when the traveler explains why the portal could not be used.
heading: Travel and Expense Policy
Overview
chunks.title: Travel and Expense Policy

chunks.body:
## Air travel

Economy class is the default for every flight. Flights longer than eight hours may be booked in premium economy without additional approval. Business class requires written approval from a vice president before the ticket is purchased. Changes to a ticket are reimbursed when the change is caused by the business purpose of the trip.
heading: Travel and Expense Policy
Air travel
chunks.title: Travel and Expense Policy

chunks.body:
## Lodging

The nightly hotel limit is 210 US dollars in most cities and 320 US dollars in the high-cost cities listed in Appendix B. Travelers who stay with friends or family may claim a flat 40 dollar hosting allowance per night instead of a hotel rate.
heading: Travel and Expense Policy
Lodging
chunks.title: Travel and Expense Policy

chunks.body:
## Meals

Meals are reimbursed at actual cost up to a daily limit of 75 US dollars. Alcohol is never reimbursed, even at a client dinner. Receipts are required for any single meal above 25 dollars.
heading: Travel and Expense Policy
Meals
chunks.title: Travel and Expense Policy

chunks.body:
## Exceptions

A manager may approve a one-time exception to the lodging limit when a conference hotel is the only reasonable option. The exception must be attached to the expense report.
heading: Travel and Expense Policy
Exceptions
chunks.title: Travel and Expense Policy

chunks.body: # Ledger Billing Service Runbook
heading: Ledger Billing Service Runbook
chunks.title: Ledger Billing Service Runbook

chunks.body:
## Overview

Ledger computes monthly invoices for every Larkspur customer and posts them to the payments provider. It runs as three replicas behind the internal load balancer.
heading: Ledger Billing Service Runbook
Overview
chunks.title: Ledger Billing Service Runbook

chunks.body:
## Alerts

The invoice-lag alert fires when the oldest unprocessed billing event is more than fifteen minutes old. The payment-rejection alert fires when more than two percent of posted invoices are rejected within an hour.
heading: Ledger Billing Service Runbook
Alerts
chunks.title: Ledger Billing Service Runbook

chunks.body:
## First response

Acknowledge the page within five minutes. Check the Ledger dashboard for queue depth, replica health and the error rate of the payments provider. If a single replica is unhealthy, drain it and let the scheduler replace it.
heading: Ledger Billing Service Runbook
First response
chunks.title: Ledger Billing Service Runbook

chunks.body:
## Detailed recovery procedure

When the invoice-lag alert persists after a replica has been replaced, the cause is usually a stuck batch rather than a capacity problem. Open the batch console and sort open batches by age. A batch that has been in the claimed state for more than twenty minutes without progress is considered stuck. Before you release a stuck batch, confirm that its worker is no longer running by checking the worker heartbeat table; releasing a batch whose worker is still alive produces duplicate invoices, which are expensive to reverse because the payments provider charges a fee for every refund. When the heartbeat is older than five minutes, release the batch with the release command and record the batch identifier in the incident channel. Released batches are claimed again by a healthy replica within a minute. If three or more batches are stuck at the same time, do not release them one by one; instead, pause the scheduler, because simultaneous stuck batches almost always indicate that the database connection pool is exhausted. Increase the pool only after the database team confirms there is headroom on the primary. After the scheduler is resumed, watch the invoice-lag graph for thirty minutes. The lag should fall steadily; a lag that falls and then plateaus means another batch has stuck and the procedure should be repeated from the beginning. Every release must be listed in the incident review with the time it was performed and the person who performed it, because finance reconciles each released batch against the payments provider's settlement report at the end of the month. If the settlement report shows a released batch that the payments provider never received, finance opens a reconciliation ticket and the billing team reposts that batch manually after confirming that no customer has been charged for it. Manual reposting is performed only by the billing team lead or a named deputy, never by the on-call engineer, because a repost bypasses the
heading: Ledger Billing Service Runbook
Detailed recovery procedure
chunks.title: Ledger Billing Service Runbook

chunks.body: after confirming that no customer has been charged for it. Manual reposting is performed only by the billing team lead or a named deputy, never by the on-call engineer, because a repost bypasses the duplicate check that normal processing performs. The on-call engineer's responsibility ends once invoices are flowing again and every release has been recorded; the follow-up reconciliation can take several days and is tracked in the finance queue rather than in the incident channel. When the same batch becomes stuck twice in one month, the billing team opens a defect for the batch worker and attaches the heartbeat history of both incidents, so that the cause can be traced to a specific worker version. Historically, most repeated stalls were traced to long-running database transactions held open by reporting queries during month-end close, which is why reporting jobs are now scheduled outside the invoicing window on the last three days of each month.
heading: Ledger Billing Service Runbook
Detailed recovery procedure
chunks.title: Ledger Billing Service Runbook

chunks.body:
## Escalation

Escalate to the billing team lead if invoices are not flowing again within one hour. Escalate to the finance director if any customer may have been charged twice.
heading: Ledger Billing Service Runbook
Escalation
chunks.title: Ledger Billing Service Runbook

chunks.body: # Q3 Customer Research Findings
heading: Q3 Customer Research Findings
chunks.title: Q3 Customer Research Findings

chunks.body:
## Overview

The research team interviewed twenty-four customers between July and September about how they use Larkspur dashboards.
heading: Q3 Customer Research Findings
Overview
chunks.title: Q3 Customer Research Findings

chunks.body:
## Key findings

Eighteen of the twenty-four customers export dashboards to spreadsheets at least weekly, mostly to combine Larkspur data with their own budget figures. Customers in healthcare asked repeatedly for audit trails that show who viewed a dashboard. Only three customers used the alerting feature, and most did not know it existed.
heading: Q3 Customer Research Findings
Key findings

chunks.body:

The most common complaint was slow loading of dashboards with more than twenty charts. Several customers described the sharing dialog as confusing because it mixes viewers and editors in one list.
heading: Q3 Customer Research Findings
Pain points

chunks.body:
## Recommendations

The team recommends a native spreadsheet connector, a viewer audit log for regulated customers, and an onboarding tour that introduces alerting.

chunks.body: # Larkspur Data API Reference
heading: Larkspur Data API Reference
chunks.title: Larkspur Data API Reference

chunks.body:
## Overview

The Larkspur Data API gives programmatic access to dashboards, datasets and query results. All endpoints use HTTPS and JSON.
heading: Larkspur Data API Reference
Overview
chunks.title: Larkspur Data API Reference

chunks.body:
## Authentication

Requests authenticate with a bearer token created in the account settings. Tokens expire after ninety days and can be revoked at any time.
heading: Larkspur Data API Reference
Authentication
chunks.title: Larkspur Data API Reference

chunks.body:
## Rate limits

Standard accounts may send 600 requests per minute. Enterprise accounts may send 3,000 requests per minute. A request over the limit receives HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds.
heading: Larkspur Data API Reference
Rate limits
chunks.title: Larkspur Data API Reference

chunks.body:
## Pagination

List endpoints return at most 200 items per page and include a cursor for the next page.
heading: Larkspur Data API Reference
Pagination
chunks.title: Larkspur Data API Reference

chunks.body:
## Versioning and deprecation

The API is versioned in the URL path, for example /v3/datasets. A version is supported for at least eighteen months after its successor is released. When a version is deprecated, every response from it carries a Deprecation header with the retirement date, and account administrators receive an email ninety days before retirement and again thirty days before retirement. Breaking changes are only ever introduced in a new version; within a version, Larkspur may add optional fields to responses and new optional parameters to requests, so clients must ignore fields they do not recognise. Error responses always contain a machine-readable code and a human-readable message, and the codes listed in the error catalogue never change meaning within a version. Clients that need longer to migrate can request an extension of up to six months through their account manager, which is granted for enterprise accounts that have a written migration plan. During an extension the retired version keeps working for that account only and is excluded from the standard availability commitment, so incidents affecting it are handled on a best-effort basis. Version three is the current version; version two was deprecated in January and retires at the end of July. After retirement, requests to a retired version receive HTTP 410 Gone with a link to the migration guide, and no data is returned. The migration guide lists every field that was renamed or removed between versions, together with the replacement field where one exists. Most clients need to change three things when moving from version two to version three: dataset identifiers are now strings rather than integers, timestamps are returned in UTC with an explicit offset, and list endpoints use cursor pagination instead of page numbers. The Python and JavaScript client libraries handle all three changes automatically from release 4.0 onwards, so clients that use a current library usually only need to upgrade the
heading: Larkspur Data API Reference
Versioning and deprecation
chunks.title: Larkspur Data API Reference

chunks.body: ead of page numbers. The Python and JavaScript client libraries handle all three changes automatically from release 4.0 onwards, so clients that use a current library usually only need to upgrade the library and run their tests. Clients that call the API directly should test against the sandbox environment, which mirrors production data structures with synthetic data and is reset every Sunday. Larkspur support can review a migration plan on request, and enterprise customers can schedule a call with an API engineer to discuss unusual integrations. Usage of each version is shown in the account's API dashboard, which helps administrators find forgotten scripts that still call an old version before it retires.
heading: Larkspur Data API Reference

chunks.body: # Postmortem: March Queue Outage
heading: Postmortem: March Queue Outage
chunks.title: Postmortem: March Queue Outage

chunks.body:
## Summary

On March 12, the ingestion queue stopped delivering events for two hours and forty minutes. Dashboards showed stale data for every customer during that time, but no data was lost.
heading: Postmortem: March Queue Outage
Summary
chunks.title: Postmortem: March Queue Outage

chunks.body:
## Impact

Roughly 1,900 customer accounts saw dashboards that were up to three hours old. Forty-one support tickets were opened.
heading: Postmortem: March Queue Outage
Impact
chunks.title: Postmortem: March Queue Outage

chunks.body:
## Timeline and root cause

At 09:05 UTC a routine certificate rotation replaced the certificate used by the queue brokers. The new certificate had been issued for the wrong internal hostname, so every consumer that reconnected after the rotation failed its TLS handshake and backed off. Because consumers reconnect gradually as their connections age, the failure did not appear all at once; delivery fell to half its normal rate at 09:40 and stopped completely at 10:20. The queue-depth alert fired at 10:25, but the on-call engineer first investigated the brokers' disk usage, which was also high because undelivered events were accumulating. At 11:05 a second engineer noticed TLS errors in the consumer logs. The previous certificate was restored at 11:30, and consumers recovered within ten minutes. The backlog of roughly forty million events was fully processed by 13:00. The certificate was wrong because the rotation tool selected a template by prefix, and a new template with a similar name had been added the week before. Nothing in the rotation process checked that the certificate matched the hostnames that clients actually use, and the staging queue, where the same rotation had run a day earlier, uses a different hostname scheme that happened to match the wrong template. During the outage, the support team posted a status page update at 10:50, thirty minutes after delivery stopped completely, and updated it every half hour until recovery. Customers who opened tickets were told that their data was delayed rather than lost, which the team could say confidently because the queue retains events for seventy-two hours. After recovery, the processing pipeline worked through the backlog at roughly three times its normal rate, which briefly raised database load on the processing side; no further alerts fired during the catch-up period. The incident commander declared the incident resolved at 13:10, once the backlog had been processed and dashboards for a sample of customers
heading: Postmortem: March Queue Outage
Timeline and root cause
chunks.title: Postmortem: March Queue Outage

chunks.body: side; no further alerts fired during the catch-up period. The incident commander declared the incident resolved at 13:10, once the backlog had been processed and dashboards for a sample of customers were confirmed to be current. A follow-up review found that the rotation tool's logs had recorded the template it selected, but nobody reviewed those logs as part of the rotation, and the tool reported success because the installation itself completed without error. The team also found that the queue-depth alert threshold had been set high to avoid noise during normal traffic peaks, which delayed detection by several minutes; the threshold is being revisited separately from the action items below.
heading: Postmortem: March Queue Outage
Timeline and root cause
chunks.title: Postmortem: March Queue Outage

chunks.body:
## Action items

Add a hostname check to the rotation tool before any certificate is installed. Alert on consumer TLS handshake failures directly. Make the staging queue use the production hostname scheme.
heading: Postmortem: March Queue Outage
Action items
chunks.title: Postmortem: March Queue Outage

chunks.body: # Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report
heading: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report
chunks.title: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report

chunks.body:
## Overview

Larkspur trialled soil moisture sensors at three farms for one growing season to test whether sensor-guided irrigation saves water without reducing yield.
heading: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report
Overview
chunks.title: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report

chunks.body:
## Sites

The trial ran at Millbrook Orchard (apples), Dunmore Fields (sweetcorn) and Ash Hollow Vineyard (grapes). Each site split its land into a sensor-guided half and a half irrigated on the farm's usual schedule.
heading: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report
Sites
chunks.title: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report

chunks.body:
## Results by site

At Millbrook Orchard, the sensor-guided half used twenty-seven percent less water than the scheduled half, and apple yield was unchanged within the margin of measurement error. The orchard manager noted that the sensors recommended skipping irrigation on several cool days in early summer when the usual schedule would have watered, and those skipped days accounted for most of the saving. At Dunmore Fields the saving was smaller, at eleven percent, because sweetcorn needs heavy watering during tasseling, and the sensors agreed with the schedule during that period; outside tasseling, the savings were similar to the orchard's. Sweetcorn yield was two percent higher on the sensor-guided half, but the difference is within the variation normally seen between fields. At Ash Hollow Vineyard, the sensor-guided half used thirty-four percent less water, the largest saving in the trial, but grape yield fell by six percent. The vineyard manager considered the lower yield acceptable because the grapes had a higher sugar content, which is valued for winemaking; however, the trial was not designed to measure grape quality, so this observation is anecdotal. Across all three sites, sensor faults were rare: four of the ninety deployed sensors failed during the season, all because of rodent damage to cables, and each failed sensor was replaced within two days. Installation took one day per site, using a crew of two technicians, and calibration against hand-held reference readings was repeated after the first month at every site. The gateways at all three sites ran on solar power without interruption, although the vineyard gateway had to be moved once because vines shaded its panel in midsummer. Data from the sensors reached the Larkspur dashboard with a median delay of four minutes, which farm managers considered more than sufficient for irrigation decisions made once or twice a day. Farm managers at all three sites reported that the dashboard's daily recommendation
heading: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report
Results by site
chunks.title: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report

chunks.body: our minutes, which farm managers considered more than sufficient for irrigation decisions made once or twice a day. Farm managers at all three sites reported that the dashboard's daily recommendation was easy to follow, but two of them asked for a weekly summary that compares water use with the previous season. The orchard manager also asked for an alert when soil moisture falls below a set level overnight, because irrigation at the orchard is often started early in the morning before staff check the dashboard. Weather during the season was close to the ten-year average, with a slightly wetter June than usual, so the results may overstate savings in a dry year; the report recommends repeating the trial over at least two further seasons before drawing firm conclusions.
heading: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report
Results by site
chunks.title: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report

chunks.body:
## Conclusions

Sensor-guided irrigation saved water at every site. Yield was unaffected for apples and sweetcorn. The effect on grapes needs a dedicated trial that measures quality as well as yield.
heading: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report
Conclusions
chunks.title: Irrigation Sensor Field Trial Report
